title: Do Kids Know How Well They Move? A Pilot  Evaluation on Perceived and Actual Motor  Competence in a Kindergarten-Based Fundamental Movement Skills Program
content: This pilot study examined embedding a fundamental movement skills (FMS) program within a kin-dergarten curriculum and explored changes in perceived motor competence (PMC) and actual motor competence (MC) pre- and post-participation. Twenty-one pre-school children (mean age = 4.94 ± 0.35 years) enrolled in a university affiliated kindergarten program completed a 12-week FMS intervention integrated into their regular kindergarten schedule. Perceived motor competence was assessed using the Pictorial Scale of Perceived Movement Skill Competence (PMSC), while actual motor competence was evaluated using the Test of Gross Motor Development-2 (TGMD-2) and Movement Assessment Battery for Children-2 (MABC-2). The children were assessed in the week prior to commencement (pre-) and the week post completion of the 12-week block of the FMS intervention.   Non-parametric analy-sis indicated no significant associations between PMC and MC at pre- or post-intervention, Baseline MC was high, with 90% of children classified as average to very superior on the TGMD-2, and 78% scoring above the 15th percentile on the MABC-2. Significant improvements from pre- to post-program participation were observed in object control skills on the TGMD-2 (z = -2.240, p = 0.025) and in the aiming and catching sub-component of the MABC-2 (z = -2.188, p = 0.029). Most children reported high PMC at baseline (>80%), which increased to 95% post-intervention.These findings suggest that the pre-school children in our sample generally demonstrate high PMC, which seems to be main-tained and supported through participation in a structured FMS program. Although direct associa-tions between PMC and MC were not evident, fostering high PMC during early childhood may sup-port ongoing motor skill development. Further research using larger and more diverse samples is re-quired to clarify the relationship between PMC and MC and to identify any contextual factors influ-encing motor development in early childhood settings.
